title: Remember My favor
hookLine: the Children of Israel are reminded of the favors given them (2:40–47)

lines: A FAMILY HEARS ITS STORY BACK.
cards: Families keep certain stories for the hard nights. The time grandpa crossed a border with one suitcase. The winter the neighbors left food on the step.
They're told so nobody forgets who they are and what was done for them.
Right after Adam, al-Baqarah speaks directly to a family, the descendants of one man, Ya'qub, also called Israel, and begins by telling their story back to them. Today: remember My favor.

teach.h: NI'MAH: A FAVOR, A GRACE GIVEN
teach.b: Verse forty, in Pickthall's words: “O Children of Israel! Remember My favour wherewith I favoured you.” The Arabic word is ni'mah, a blessing, a grace given. The verse goes on: keep your covenant, and I will keep Mine.
The next stretch of al-Baqarah, many pages of it, is that remembering. You were rescued from Pharaoh, who was killing your sons. The sea was parted for you.

You were shaded with clouds in the desert, and fed with manna and quails. Water burst from a rock in twelve springs, one for each tribe. These are stories Jews also tell, from their own scripture, in their own words.
The Qur'an tells them back with honor and with honesty: alongside the gifts, it remembers the calf, the grumbling, the broken promises, the way any family history includes both.
Why would a book addressed to the whole world speak so long to one people?
Some commentators answer: because the pattern is for everyone. A community is given much, makes a covenant, remembers or forgets. Muslim teachers read these passages as a warning to Muslims too.
And the first instruction isn't obey. It's remember.

teach.h: GRATITUDE IS A KIND OF MEMORY
teach.b: Gratitude, in this verse, is a kind of memory: a promise is hard to keep to someone whose kindness has been forgotten.
Remember the favor, and the covenant becomes something you keep because you remember, not only because you're told.

how: Muslims read al-Baqarah's long address to the Children of Israel as part of the Qur'an's teaching to every community, and naming blessings aloud with alhamdulillah is a common habit.

o: a favor, a blessing, a grace given
the manna that fell in the desert
a covenant that binds both sides

games.q: you're reminding someone of a promise they made to you. where does verse forty start?
o: with the punishment for breaking it.
with the favor that was given.
games.why: with the favor: remember, then keep your covenant and I will keep Mine. gratitude comes before the promise.

practice: Bring to mind three favors given to you, specific ones with names and places: the teacher who stayed late, the stranger who found your wallet, the night someone drove two hours to sit with you.
Stay with each one for a few breaths, and if you pray, you can say alhamdulillah after each.

wordCard.voice: Ni'mah. A favor, a blessing given — what al-Baqarah tells the Children of Israel, and all of us, to remember before keeping a covenant. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a favor, a blessing, a grace given; the word in 2:40.

carryVoice: Your line: remember the favor. Gratitude, in this verse, starts as memory. Day three hundred forty, done.
